The excellent combination of strength and ductility for the alloy at 77 K relative to 298 K is mainly attributed to a more significant TRIP effect.

the HCP phase became the dominant component in the fractured A10 alloy, suggesting that deformation-induced phase transformation acts as the dominant deformation mechanism of the A10 alloy at 298 and 77 K

the alloy deformed at 77 K showed a higher fraction of HCP phase than that at 298 K with the same level of tensile strain (e.g., ε = 15%), indicating that the alloy exhibited a more significant TRIP effect

The formation of DTs and the HCP phase introduced some new interfaces which refined the microstructure and reduced the mean free path of dislocation slip during tensile deformation, providing dynamic Hall-Petch hardening to the alloy
the grain-boundary strengthening effect plays an important role in improving the mechanical behavior of the as-sintered alloys
the Mn oxide particles with FCC structure had a strong blocking effect on the dislocation movement and generated strengthening by a dislocation bypass mechanism (Orowan mechanism)
many twins were annihilated due to the detwinning process through the interaction of the dislocations with the TBs leading to a significant decrease in TBs fraction

During tensile deformation at 298 K, dislocation slip, phase transformation, detwinning of annealing twins, and mechanical twinning were the dominant mechanisms
Dense grain boundaries can inhibit the growth of twins and the HCP phase
The increase in grain size leads to a decrease in the fraction of grain boundaries, which reduces the resistance of dislocation movement and decreases the strength of the alloy
It is suggested that the increase in HCP phase fraction is caused by the deformation-induced phase transformation from FCC to HCP.
the smaller the grain size, the higher the grain-boundary strengthening, which can be explained by the Hall-Petch effect, leading to an increase in the YS
